transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-07 16:00 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Marcus Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Tom Alvarez (CISO - StellarLogix), Jenna Park (Cloud Eng), Ravi Singh (Data Privacy Counsel), Maya Ortiz (CTO)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on governance and security requirements for evaluating Redwood's hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment options. High interest in KMS/HSM integration, audit logs, RBAC/SSO, data retention and eDiscovery, and SOC2/ISO evidence. Customer wants clear migration and pilot plan before procurement.

Topics: SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, SSO / SAML, RBAC, audit logs retention, encryption/KMS/HSM, VPC/private deployment, data residency and retention policies, legal hold, pilot scope, benchmarking.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Marcus: hey everybody thanks for joining, this is Marcus from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account. quick intro?
[00:07] Tom: hi tom alvarez here ciso, quick heads up we have tight timelines, want to know what kind of evidence and controls you provide.
[00:12] Maya: maya ortiz, CTO, mostly here to hear about private deployment options and whether we can run inference in our VPC.
[00:18] Jenna: jenna park, cloud eng, i'll be point on integration and kms.
[00:22] Ravi: ravi singh, data privacy counsel, i'll focus on retention and legal hold needs.
[00:26] Priya: priya from redwood se, i'll cover technical questions and followups on private/dedicated architecture.

[00:40] Marcus: to frame the convo — are you leaning hosted first or straight to dedicated/private? where are you in procurement?
[00:45] Tom: we want to evaluate hosted to get moving but procurement will push for private or dedicated if security gaps show. SOC2 is table stakes, ISO would be nice.
[00:55] Maya: budget will allow a pilot on dedicated if the economics look right. long term, private may be required for certain regulated workloads.

[01:10] Jenna: our infra currently sits in aws us-west-2. we use KMS CMKs for data at rest. question — can we bring our own KMS/HSM or does Redwood manage keys?
[01:20] Priya: good question. for hosted we offer a Redwood-managed KMS by default, and we also support customer-managed keys in many cases via Cloud KMS integrations, and for Private we can integrate with your on-prem HSM or KMS; there are a couple of options depending on deployment model.
[01:40] Tom: is there a bring-your-own-key (BYOK) flow documented? and does Redwood support HSM-backed keys so keys never leave our control?
[01:48] Priya: yes, there is a BYOK flow. for Private we support HSMs and there's a pattern we use where the control plane talks to your KMS over the VPC peering or private link. i'll share the runbook.

[02:10] Ravi: about audit logs — how granular are they? do you capture per-request metadata, including model, route, token counts, requester id, ip, latency? we need these for forensic and compliance.
[02:22] Marcus: we provide per-request audit logging in Dedicated and Private, hosted has application level logs and admin level logs — but we can push expanded logging for enterprise tiers. priya — correct me on fields.
[02:31] Priya: sure, typical audit log entries include timestamp, request id, model id, tenant id, route, requester identity (if SSO), high-level token usage but not full content by default for privacy reasons. for Private you can enable full request payload retention if you want, and logs can be forwarded to customer SIEM.

[02:55] Tom: forwarding to our SIEM is critical. we run splunk and var audit pipeline. can logs be streamed in near real-time?
[03:03] Priya: yes, we stream via syslog or kafka depending on your stack; near real-time is supported. retention windows are configurable in Dedicated/Private. hosted has default 90 days for certain logs but enterprise retention add-ons are available.

[03:25] Jenna: what about RBAC and SSO? we use okta and SAML for staff access, but we also have service principals for our apps.
[03:32] Marcus: we support SSO with SAML and OIDC, SCIM provisioning for users, and RBAC with roles that can be scoped to projects and models. priya, can you run through admin roles vs developer roles?
[03:42] Priya: admin role includes org level permissions: billing, audit, user mgmt. developer role can create routes and call models but not change org settings. we also support API keys for service principals, and keys can be rotated. in private deployment you map roles to your idp groups.

[04:15] Tom: audit trail for admin changes — do you keep who changed RBAC and when? we need immutability for a period of time.
[04:22] Priya: yes, admin actions are logged with who/when/what, and in Dedicated/Private we can set write-once retention policies for those logs and ship to your long term archive.

[04:40] Ravi: data residency — some datasets cannot leave eu, do you offer region restrictions?
[04:47] Marcus: Redwood supports hosted in multiple regions, Dedicated can be provisioned in region-specific pools, and Private obviously runs in your VPC or on-prem. for eu-only data we'd recommend Dedicated in eu region or Private.

[05:05] Maya: what's the default retention for request content in hosted? i heard some vendors keep prompts for 30 days.
[05:12] Priya: hosted retains non-sensitive telemetry by default 90 days, request content is not retained by default for standard hosted customers — but enterprise tiers may have opt-in content retention for auditing. we'll include precise defaults in the docs we send.

[05:35] Jenna: eDiscovery / legal hold — we sometimes need to put preservation holds for months. can you support pausing auto-deletes?
[05:43] Priya: yes, in Dedicated/Private you control retention policies and we can pause deletion for specified sets of request ids. for hosted we'll need a legal process flow; it's supported with enterprise agreements.

[06:05] Tom: encryption in transit — mTLS between services? we require mutual TLS for certain endpoints.
[06:12] Priya: we support TLS1.2+ and mTLS for Private peered endpoints. hosted api endpoints are TLS; for stricter requirements we recommend Private or Dedicated with private network peering.

[06:32] Ravi: difficult question — if there's a subpoena, how do you handle data requests? who has access to logs and payloads?
[06:40] Marcus: Redwood's policy is to follow legal process; for hosted we handle requests per our privacy policy and customer notification terms; for Private deployments your legal team retains control because data is in your environment. we'll surface our standard legal process in the SOC2 docs.

[07:05] Maya: operationally, we want a canary and rollback strategy. how do rollouts look across dedicated pools — do you support canary percentages and automatic fallback?
[07:14] Priya: yes, our runtime supports canary rollouts, traffic splitting, and automated fallback to a compatible variant if latency or errors exceed thresholds. these are in Redwood Console and configurable per route.

[07:40] Tom: a couple of nuanced items — do you do model-level auditing (who invoked which model) and KV cache interactions? are cache hits logged?
[07:50] Priya: model invocations are logged; cache hits are captured as part of the request metadata when caching is enabled. small caveat — KV cache content is not stored in audit logs unless explicitly enabled in Private deployments for debugging.

[08:20] Jenna: integration detail: if we want our KMS to sign tokens so that keys never leave our control, what's the flow?
[08:28] Priya: we typically use envelope encryption where the CMK protects the data encryption keys; for private/HSM we will set up a flow where the KMS holds key material and Redwood's runtime requests key operations over a secure channel, keys don't leave your HSM. i'll add the whitepaper link.

[09:05] Ravi: can you attest to separation of duties? we need to show that ops personnel can't access customer data casually.
[09:12] Marcus: separation of duties is documented in our compliance materials; we have role-based internal access controls and limited access to prod logs. SOC2 controls cover that — we'll send the control mapping.

[09:40] Maya: encryption at rest, algorithm details—what ciphers, and do you support customer-specified algorithms?
[09:47] Priya: standard AES-256-GCM for data at rest; for Private you can bring custom crypto solutions via HSM. we'll include algorithm details in the doc set.

[10:15] Tom: any past incidents we should know about? incident history and timeline?
[10:20] Marcus: we disclose incident history in SOC2 report and in our trust portal; we have a public status page and a security page and we'll share the timeline for past incidents with mitigating controls.

[10:40] Jenna: request: do you have a hardened image for on-prem, or is private a containerized deployment we run?
[10:48] Priya: Private is an appliance-like package: containerized runtime plus an optional management plane. we provide a hardened baseline and Ansible terraform scripts for deployment. we'll share a deployment checklist.

[11:18] Ravi: SLA question — uptime guarantees and notification windows?
[11:24] Marcus: Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime targets; Private is covered under enterprise license terms. we'll include SLA language and severity definitions.

[11:45] Maya: performance benchmarking — we want latency P95 under 200ms for small prompts. can you support benchmarking in our environment?
[11:54] Priya: yes, we offer benchmark runs as a pilot — we can spin up dedicated capacity in your region and run synthetic and replay-based tests. results feed into model/quantization recommendations.

[12:20] Tom: who would be our escalation contact for security incidents?
[12:25] Marcus: primary security escalation would be our security lead on call; we'll provide names and pgp keys if needed.

[12:45] Jenna: are there any managed backup features for config and logs? we want disaster recovery for audit trails.
[12:53] Priya: logs can be exported to your archival storage (s3 glacial, etc.), and config backups are supported with versioning.

[13:18] Tommy (interrupt, misattributed speaker tag): sorry, tiny thing, does the hosted tier allow IP allow-listing?
[13:24] Marcus: yes, hosted supports IP allow-listing for API keys in enterprise tiers.

[13:40] Tom: procurement note — we need vendor risk assessment info, SSAE and SOC docs, ISO summary, encryption attestation, and customer references in regulated industries.
[13:52] Marcus: understood. we'll collate that and send it after.

[14:10] Priya: quick follow up on deployment models — dedicated is reserved GPU pools managed by Redwood in your chosen region; private is a package that runs in your network with optional control plane connectivity. both have stronger log and KMS integration than hosted.

[14:45] Maya: for private, what are common timelines to get through onboarding and pilot?
[14:52] Priya: typically 6-8 weeks for Private (security review, network setup, deployment), 2-4 weeks for Dedicated pilot depending on capacity. procurement and legal can add lead time.

[15:10] Ravi: data deletion certification — can you provide a signed attestation after data purge?
[15:16] Marcus: yes, for Dedicated/Private we can provide a deletion certificate and audit trail of purge activities.

[15:35] Jenna: we use role-separated service accounts; are API key uses logged per-service account?
[15:40] Priya: yes, API key and service principal usage are logged and can be mapped back to a principal id.

[16:00] Tom: any third-party vendor subprocessing — who else has access to data?
[16:06] Marcus: third-party subprocessors are listed in the DPA; typical ones include cloud infra providers and monitoring vendors; hosted will use some managed services; we'll share the latest subprocessor list.

[16:30] Maya: cost vs security tradeoffs — our finance will want hard numbers for dedicated vs private.
[16:36] Marcus: we'll provide detailed estimates in the pricing sheet. dedicated is generally more predictable; private can have higher upfront costs but better isolation.

[16:55] Priya: quick note — for customers with strict key custody we recommend Private with HSM integration; for teams ok with managed keys dedicated with customer-managed key integration may be a good compromise.

[17:20] Tom: last thing — do you do penetration testing and allow customer-initiated PT?
[17:27] Marcus: we do internal pentests and annual 3rd party assessments; customer-initiated pentests are allowed under a coordinated disclosure policy — we'll share the process.

[17:50] Maya: ok that covers our questions. next steps are as earlier — SOC2 docs, tech deep dive, pricing, and the security questionnaire.

[18:05] Marcus: perfect i'll get those across. any blockers on scheduling the deep dive?
[18:10] Jenna: week of 4/13 works.
[18:14] Priya: i'll send a calendar invite and agenda.

Recap / Closing:
[18:30] Marcus: recap — action items: i will send SOC2/ISO docs and subprocessor list; priya will set up tech deep dive for private deployment and benchmark options; jenna and ravi will share infra diagram and retention/legal hold requirements. we aim to reconvene after the deep dive with a pilot plan.
[18:55] Tom: thanks all, appreciate the clarity.
[19:00] Maya: thanks.
[19:05] Marcus: thanks everyone, talk soon.

Notes on transcript quality: automatic transcription with occasional mislabels (e.g., KV caching as 'KV cashe', 'SAML' sometimes as 'Sam el'), filler words and interruptions preserved.
